claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start the assessment process.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! I'm starting your Child Benefit eligibility assessment. 

First, I need to know about the child or children you're claiming for. Let me gather some information:

**What is the age of the child you're claiming for?**

Please let me know:
- The child's current age, or their date of birth
- If you have multiple children, please tell me about each one

The rules for Child Benefit differ depending on whether the child is:
- **Under 16 years old**
- **16-19 years old** (depends on education/training)
- **20 years old or over** (not eligible)

Once you provide the age, I can guide you through the next steps.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Hi, yes, I'm interested in claiming Child Benefit and wanted to check if I'm eligible.

I have one child - Alex, who is 17 years old and lives with me at home.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! So you have **Alex, who is 17 years old** and lives with you. Since Alex is 16-19 years old, I need to check some additional requirements related to education or training.

Let me get the details I need:

**Is Alex currently in full-time education or an approved training course?**

For Child Benefit purposes, 16-19 year olds must be:
- In full-time education (such as secondary school, college, or university), OR
- On an approved training course

Can you confirm whether Alex is in full-time education or training, and if so, what type?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Alex isn't in college or anything like that. He's actually started an apprenticeship recently - he's training in carpentry.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying! Alex is on an apprenticeship, which is an approved training course. That's helpful information.

Now I need to check one more important requirement for 16-19 year olds:

**Is Alex working full-time (16 hours or more per week) while on the apprenticeship?**

The reason I'm asking is that there are specific rules about how many hours can be worked. Let me navigate based on what you tell me.

How many hours per week is Alex working as part of the apprenticeship?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, he's working full-time as part of the apprenticeship - it's a proper job with training included.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. Before I continue, I need to clarify the exact hours to make sure I apply the right rules.

**How many hours per week is Alex working?** Is it:
- Between 16-29 hours per week, or
- 30 hours or more per week?

This is important because the Child Benefit rules have different thresholds for working hours during apprenticeships and training.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: It's more than 24 hours a week - he's there full-time, so I'd say around 30 to 35 hours a week.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying. So Alex is working 30-35 hours per week on a full-time apprenticeship.

Now let me navigate through the eligibility check with this information.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Good, so Alex is in training. Now let me continue:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check the details of Alex's apprenticeship training to see if it meets the approved education criteria.

**I need to understand more about Alex's apprenticeship:**

1. **What qualification level is Alex working towards?** For example:
   - Is it an NVQ (and if so, what level - 1, 2, 3, or 4+)?
   - Is it a different type of qualification?

2. **Is the apprenticeship funded by an employer** (rather than publicly funded through a scheme like the Apprenticeship Levy)?

3. **How many hours per week is Alex doing supervised study or training** (not just practical work)? The requirement is at least 12 hours per week of supervised study.

This information will help me determine if Alex's apprenticeship counts as "approved education" for Child Benefit purposes.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: It's a carpentry apprenticeship - I believe it's an NVQ Level 2 or 3. Yes, it's through his employer, a local building company. As for the supervised study, I'm not entirely sure of the exact breakdown, but he does attend college one day a week for the theory side of things, and the rest is on-site training with supervision from qualified carpenters.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that detailed information. Let me clarify a couple of important points about the supervised study requirement:

**Regarding the supervised study hours:**
Alex attends college one day a week for theory - that's good. The on-site training with qualified carpenters also counts as supervised study. 

Let me ask: **How many hours per week in total would you estimate Alex is doing supervised study or training?** Is it:
- At least 12 hours per week (which would meet the requirement), or
- Less than 12 hours per week?

One day a week at college plus on-site supervision typically adds up to well over 12 hours, so I want to confirm this is the case.

Also, **one more important clarification:** You mentioned the apprenticeship is through his employer. Is this:
- A standard apprenticeship program (publicly funded/regulated), or
- Something the employer is funding entirely on their own for a specific job they have agreed on with Alex?

This distinction matters because employer-funded training that's agreed as part of a future job contract can affect eligibility.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Well, the college day is about 6-7 hours, and then during the week on-site he's being supervised and trained by the qualified carpenters - so I'd say that's easily more than 12 hours total per week of proper training and study.

As for the funding, it's a proper apprenticeship program - you know, the official kind. He had to apply for it and everything. It's not just something the company made up themselves.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent, thank you for clarifying. So Alex has:
- **NVQ Level 2 or 3 in carpentry** (which is approved - below Level 4)
- **More than 12 hours per week of supervised study/training** (college day plus on-site supervision)
- **A proper, official apprenticeship program** (not employer-funded in the excluded sense)

This is looking good. Now I need to check the final key requirement for 16-19 year olds:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Now I need to check one more thing about Alex's work hours:

**You mentioned earlier that Alex is working 30-35 hours per week. This is important for the final eligibility check.**

The question is: **Is Alex working less than 24 hours per week, or is he working 24+ hours per week?**

Based on what you said (30-35 hours), it sounds like he's working 24+ hours per week. Can you confirm this is correct?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, that's right - he's working more than 24 hours a week. Like I said, it's a full-time apprenticeship, so around 30-35 hours.

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for confirming. I understand Alex is working 30-35 hours per week as part of his full-time apprenticeship.

I need to clarify an important point about the rules: **Is Alex in full-time approved education or training (meaning 12+ hours per week of supervised study/training)?**

You mentioned he attends college one day a week (6-7 hours) plus on-site supervision. The key question is: **Does this on-site training count as formal, approved education/training supervised by qualified instructors, or is it primarily practical work experience?**

For Child Benefit purposes, there's a distinction between:
- **Approved education/training** (formal instruction that counts toward a qualification)
- **Paid work** (even if it includes on-the-job training)

In the case of an apprenticeship, the college day definitely counts as approved training. But I need to understand if the total supervised study time (college + on-site instruction) genuinely meets the 12+ hours per week requirement for **approved education**, or if much of his time is considered paid work.

Can you help clarify: Is Alex primarily in an approved training program (with work as part of it), or is he primarily working full-time with some training included?

This is important because the rules differ significantly between these scenarios.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, it's an official apprenticeship program - so yes, it's a proper training program where he's working towards his NVQ qualification. The college day is definitely formal education, and the on-site work is part of the training requirement for the apprenticeship. He's learning the trade under qualified carpenters. It's not like he's just working a regular job - the whole point is that he's training to become a qualified carpenter. That's how apprenticeships work, isn't it?

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
You're absolutely right - that's exactly how apprenticeships work, and I appreciate you clarifying that. Alex is in an official apprenticeship program working towards an NVQ qualification, with both formal college instruction and structured on-the-job training. That's clearly an approved training program.

However, I need to check one more important rule that applies specifically to 16-19 year olds in training who are also working significant hours.

Let me get the specific constants and rules to make sure I'm applying this correctly:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I've just reviewed the specific rules, and I need to give you important information about Alex's eligibility.

Looking at the apprenticeship rules in the specification, I can see that:

**In England:** ALL types of apprenticeships (Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, and Degree Apprenticeships) disqualify a child from Child Benefit eligibility - even if they're also in approved education/training.

Since Alex is on a carpentry apprenticeship in England, this unfortunately means he **does not qualify for Child Benefit**, regardless of the fact that:
- He's working towards an NVQ Level 2 or 3 (which would normally be approved)
- He's getting formal college instruction
- He's under 20 years old

The rule is that apprenticeships in England are specifically excluded from Child Benefit eligibility.

**However, I want to double-check one thing:** Is Alex located in England, Scotland, or Wales? The rules differ by country:
- **England:** All apprenticeships excluded
- **Scotland:** Modern Apprenticeships excluded
- **Wales:** Foundation Apprenticeships are approved (but other apprenticeships are excluded)

Can you confirm which country Alex is in?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Yes, we live in England - I'm in Manchester, like I mentioned at the start.

So you're saying that because it's an apprenticeship in England, Alex doesn't qualify for Child Benefit at all? Even though he's only 17 and doing proper training?

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Yes, I'm afraid that's correct, and I understand this is disappointing news. According to the official Child Benefit eligibility rules, **all apprenticeships in England are excluded from qualifying**, regardless of the apprentice's age or the quality of the training.

This is a specific exclusion in the regulations, even though apprenticeships do include formal education and training. The fact that Alex is 17, doing an NVQ qualification, and attending college as part of his apprenticeship doesn't override this particular rule.

Let me provide you with the formal eligibility outcome:

conversation.author: child_benefit_eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
## Result: **NOT ELIGIBLE**

I'm sorry to deliver this outcome. Here's what you need to know:

**Why Alex doesn't qualify:**
- Alex is on an apprenticeship in England, and the Child Benefit rules specifically exclude all apprenticeships in England from eligibility
- This applies to all apprenticeship levels (Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, and Degree)
- It doesn't matter that the apprenticeship includes formal education—the exclusion applies across the board

**Important notes:**
- This is a specific regulatory exclusion, not a reflection on the quality or legitimacy of Alex's apprenticeship training
- If Alex were in Wales on a **Foundation Apprenticeship**, he would qualify—but regular apprenticeships in Wales are also excluded
- This rule applies only to apprenticeships; if Alex moves into other forms of full-time education (like college or sixth form) after completing the apprenticeship, the situation could change

**What you can do:**
- If you believe there may be exceptional circumstances or if you'd like to discuss this further, you can contact **HMRC Child Benefit Office** on **0300 200 3100**
- You can also apply directly and let HMRC make a formal decision, though based on the current rules, the outcome would be the same

I'm sorry this wasn't the news you were hoping for. Is there anything else I can help clarify about this ruling?

age_limits.birthday_rule: Benefit stops on child's 20th birthday, not end of academic year

training_exclusions: Training with employer agreement for future job

payment_rates.note: Current rates not specified in source documents - check gov.uk for latest rates

high_income_charge.note: High Income Child Benefit Charge applies if you or partner earns over £60,000. This is a payment adjustment, not an eligibility criterion.

age_and_education.rule: Child must be under 16, OR aged 16-19 and in approved education or training
age_and_education.approved_education: Full-time non-advanced education (12+ hours/week supervised study): A-levels, T-levels, Scottish Highers, NVQ Level 3 or below
age_and_education.advanced_education_excluded: University degrees, HNC (Level 4), HND (Level 5), NVQ Level 4+, professional qualifications Level 4+
age_and_education.minimum_hours: 12 hours per week supervised study required for 16-19 year olds
age_and_education.approved_training: Unpaid work-based training with education provider, or approved training course. Employer-funded training excluded.
age_and_education.extension: If 16-17 year old leaves education/training, benefit continues for 20 weeks if registered with careers service, Connexions, or armed services. Ends at week 20 or age 18, whichever sooner.
age_and_education.birthday_cutoff: Benefit stops on child's 20th birthday, not at end of academic year
age_and_education.married_children: Married 16-19 year olds only qualify if financially dependent on claimant
ending_conditions: Child starts paid work 24+ hours per week and leaves education/training
Child receives ESA, Universal Credit, or similar benefits in own right
Child starts advanced education (university, HNC, HND)

apprenticeship_rules.england: ALL apprenticeships disqualify (Intermediate, Advanced, Higher, Degree)
apprenticeship_rules.wales: Foundation Apprenticeships APPROVED. Other Welsh apprenticeships disqualify.
apprenticeship_rules.note: Welsh Foundation Apprenticeships are the ONLY apprenticeships that qualify for Child Benefit

residency.rule: Must normally live in UK or meet special circumstances
residency.settled_status: Can claim with settled status under EU Settlement Scheme
presettled_status_conditions: Working and earning above NI primary threshold for 3 continuous months, OR
Looking for work (jobseeker for up to 91 days), OR
Sufficient resources (not claiming IS, JSA, PC, UC), OR
Family member of EEA/Swiss national with right to reside
residency.abroad: May qualify if Crown servant or living in certain countries

responsibility.rule: Must be responsible for child through living with them OR contributing to upkeep
responsibility.contributing: Must pay at least Child Benefit amount (or equivalent in kind) towards care
responsibility.contribution_threshold: £26.05 per week for eldest/only child, £17.25 per week for additional children (2024/25 rates - check gov.uk for current rates)
responsibility.frequency: Can be weekly, monthly, or lump sum
responsibility.combined_contributions: Two people can combine contributions if both contribute to same child

unequal_allocation.rule: When contributing to multiple children, can allocate contribution amounts unequally
unequal_allocation.explanation: If contributing £40 for two children, can allocate as £26.05 (eldest) + £13.95 (second), or any split where each child receives at least their applicable rate
unequal_allocation.example_1: £40 total for 2 children: £26.05 (child 1) + £13.95 (child 2) = eligible for child 1 only
unequal_allocation.example_2: £50 total for 2 children: £26.05 (child 1) + £23.95 (child 2) = eligible for both
unequal_allocation.note: Each child must receive at least the Child Benefit rate they would generate (eldest rate for first child, additional rate for others)

responsibility.adoption_allowance: Adoption allowance does NOT disqualify (unlike fostering allowance)

priority_rules.rule: Only one person can claim Child Benefit for a child
priority_rules.multiple_carers: If two people are responsible, they must agree who claims

hmrc_arbitration.rule: If agreement cannot be reached, HMRC decides based on evidence
criteria: Primary residence (where child spends most nights per week)
Main contributor to child's upkeep and care
Stability and continuity for the child
evidence_required: Proof of residence (utility bills, rental agreement, council tax)
Financial contribution evidence (bank statements, receipts, maintenance records)
Court orders or formal custody arrangements (if applicable)
Statements from child's school, doctor, or other professionals
common_scenarios: Separated parents with child spending 4 days vs 3 days per week with each
Grandparent caring for grandchild while parent works
Child living part-time with two different households
Parent vs step-parent both contributing significantly
hmrc_arbitration.appeal_process: Contact Child Benefit Office if circumstances change significantly

priority_rules.transfer: Current claimant can transfer by contacting Child Benefit Office
priority_rules.child_moves: If child moves but you still contribute to upkeep (at least CB amount), you can continue claiming

hospital.time_limit: 12 weeks in hospital or residential accommodation
hospital.linking_rule: CUMULATIVE: If child returns within 28 days, time counts towards 12-week limit. Multiple stays within 28 days add together.
hospital.example: 10 weeks + 15 day gap + 3 weeks = 13 weeks cumulative (exceeds limit)
hospital.exception: Can continue if regularly spending money on child
hospital.abroad: For hospital abroad, only if went for treatment and you're back in UK spending on them
hospital.mental_health: Psychiatric units count as hospital, not custody

care.exception_24_hours: Can continue if child spends 24+ hours per week at home
care.exception_nights: Can continue if child spends 2 consecutive nights per week at home
care.reclaim_conditions: Can claim again if child spends 2 consecutive nights/week OR 7+ consecutive days at home
care.custody: Youth custody counts as care, 8-week limit applies

hospital_and_care.partner_spending: Partner's money only counts if married/civil partnered and living together

council_payments.rule: Generally cannot claim if local council is paying for child's accommodation or maintenance
council_payments.fostering: Can claim for fostered child only if council NOT paying
council_payments.informal_care: Cannot claim if council paying for informal care arrangement

administrative.backdating: Claims can be backdated up to 3 months

high_income_charge.rule: HICBC is a payment adjustment, not an eligibility criterion. Claimant is still eligible but may owe tax.
high_income_charge.calculation: Tax charge = 1% of Child Benefit for every £200 of income between £60k-£80k
high_income_charge.who_pays: Higher earner in household pays, regardless of who claims Child Benefit
examples: Income £80,000+: 100% clawback (but still eligible, just repay full amount)
high_income_charge.opt_out: Can choose not to receive payments to avoid charge, but should still register to protect National Insurance credits
high_income_charge.partner_income: Partner's income applies even if they are not the claimant. Higher earner always pays.
high_income_charge.not_eligibility: Important: HICBC does NOT affect eligibility. It is a post-payment tax charge only.

payment_structure.eldest_child_rate: Higher rate for first child claimed
payment_structure.additional_children_rate: Lower rate for each additional child
payment_structure.split_family_rule: If two parents each claim for different children from same family, both get eldest child rate for their first child
payment_structure.example: Divorced parents: Mother claims for child A (gets eldest rate), Father claims for child B (also gets eldest rate, not additional rate)
payment_structure.frequency: Paid every 4 weeks, or weekly if single parent or receiving certain benefits
